item.title: When bureaucracy gives you something it shouldn't
item.description:
Epistemic status: two cases and the statute behind them. The first case rests on one side's account in a lawyer's call-in video; I have not seen her file. I am not a lawyer. I could not find a base rate.

AI use: a Codex session did the research: pulled the video captions, found the Policy Manual section and the Turfah opinion plus related cases, and summed the fiscal year 2025 totals from USCIS's spreadsheet. Claude then fact-checked every claim against the primary sources, proofread, and wrote the footnotes. The text and the opinions are mine.

Bureaucracy is a complex and well-oiled machine. But the individual parts of it are still humans, who make mistakes. I stumbled upon this video, which I found an interesting example of this.[1]It is a conversation between an immigration attorney and a Canadian woman. She married an American citizen and applied for a green card because of that. However, for religious reasons she didn't want to get a tetanus shot. This was already surprising to me - I didn't know there was a religious exception to vaccination when immigrating to the US.[2]Her adviser at the time (not the attorney in the call, and not an attorney at all) told her that in order to achieve this she should apply as normal, without proof of vaccination. USCIS would then send her an RFE (request for evidence) for the vaccination proof, and she would submit a special form requesting the religious exception. It is unclear whether this would have worked at all, because USCIS only grants the religious exception if you refuse all vaccines, i.e. you cannot pick and choose, and in the call it sounded like she didn't want the tetanus one specifically.[3]It is also not explained why it was done this way; apparently one can just include this form in the original application.[4]According to the story, USCIS just approved the application without the RFE, the vaccination or the religious waiver. The adviser told the lady that this was the discretion of the immigration officer, but apparently this was just a mistake. Then, years later, the lady tries to naturalize (obtain US citizenship), which requires more scrutiny from USCIS,[5]and during the interview they discover that her green card was unlawfully obtained, since she never completed this requirement, and that she shouldn't have received the green card in the first place. They deny the application.[6]

This denial is in agreement with the law as it is read. INA §318 / 8 U.S.C. §1429 requires that the applicant was "lawfully admitted to the United States for permanent residence in accordance with all applicable provisions" of the immigration law. The statute itself says nothing about mistakes; the reading that a mistaken approval is not a lawful one comes from the Board of Immigration Appeals and the courts that deferred to it,[7]and USCIS has written it into its Policy Manual. USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 12, Part D, Chapter 2, section A.5, titled "U.S. Government Error", explicitly says that one is not eligible for naturalization

"if his or her LPR status was obtained in error, even in the absence of fraud or willful misrepresentation."

(LPR is lawful permanent resident, i.e. a green card holder.)[8]

I find this surprising, because effectively this says "when a system has an error, it is the applicant's problem". In Turfah v. United States Citizenship & Immigration Services, which upheld such a denial and which I will consider below (it is a different case from the video above), the court called Turfah's circumstances "certainly sympathetic" and conceded that the result "could be considered unfair", but held that it was "constrained" to follow the regulation.[9]

I wasn't able to find a well-defined remedy for this woman's case. Even if she were somehow able to provide the vaccination or the religious exception now, there is still the question of her original residence date, which defines when she will be able to naturalize.[10]

I found Kamal Turfah's case from 2017.[11]In 1995, Turfah entered the US on an immigrant visa which depended on his father's immigration. The requirement of the visa was to accompany his father or enter afterwards. However, Turfah entered 24 days before his father and was admitted nevertheless. In 2012, after 17 years, Turfah applied for citizenship, which USCIS denied because Turfah had entered the US before his father, violating the visa requirements. In January 2017 the Sixth Circuit court upheld the decision. The district court (Judge Battani) had proposed a remedy: Turfah applying for a new adjustment of status, which USCIS could at its discretion approve retroactively (this was just a suggestion). According to Judge Boggs's concurrence, "there is no explicit mechanism for an immigrant who already has LPR status to petition for an adjustment so as to be deemed 'lawfully admitted'", and he added the irony that filing the adjustment application (Form I-485) "would possibly require at least a momentary determination that Turfah does not presently have LPR status".[12]

It is natural to view USCIS negatively in light of these cases. However, these seem to be rare exceptions. In fiscal year 2025 USCIS completed about 11 million cases, including about 984,000 naturalization applications, of which about 86,000 were denied for any reason.[13]Obviously there are no stats on the number of denials due to government mistake. Based on the number of described cases online it looks negligible compared to the total, though this is weak evidence: almost nobody litigates a naturalization denial, so most such cases would leave no public trace. Obviously, for the person affected by such a denial, it is a huge problem.

  1. ^

    "USCIS Says My Green Card Was Issued by Mistake. What Happens with My Naturalization?", Hacking Immigration Law, LLC, Immigration Answers Show, uploaded 5 May 2026, 19 minutes. The host is attorney Jim Hacking. The caller's account is the only source for her facts. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QyD_-I1ABog

  2. ^

    INA 212(g)(2)(C), 8 U.S.C. 1182(g)(2)(C): the vaccination requirement may be waived where it "would be contrary to the alien's religious beliefs or moral convictions". The form is I-601 (Application for Waiver of Grounds of Inadmissibility). Tetanus is on the statutory list of required vaccines in 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(1)(A)(ii). https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1182

  3. ^

    USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 9, Part D, Chapter 3, section E.2: "The applicant must be opposed to all vaccinations in any form", the objection "must be based on religious beliefs or moral convictions" and "must be sincere"; "the applicant cannot 'pick and choose' between the vaccinations." https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-9-part-d-chapter-3 . In the video she says (00:33) "I was not wanting to get my tetanus shot because I felt, you know, a religious conviction against that", and names no other vaccine.

  4. ^

    USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 8, Part B, Chapter 12: applicants "must file a waiver application either along with their Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status (Form I-485) and Report of Immigration Medical Examination and Vaccination Record (Form I-693) or in response to a Request for Evidence." https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-8-part-b-chapter-12

  5. ^

    USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 12, Part D, Chapter 2, section D: "During a naturalization proceeding, the officer must verify the underlying immigrant visa petition ... or other basis for immigrating that formed the basis of the adjustment of status", and "USCIS may find that the applicant was not lawfully admitted to the United States for permanent residence." Section A.1: the lawful-admission requirement "applies to the applicant's initial admission as a lawful permanent resident (LPR) or adjustment to LPR status." https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-12-part-d-chapter-2

  6. ^

    Timeline from the video: green card approved in 2021 (00:23); naturalization interview in early 2026, where the officer asked at the end whether she had ever filed the waiver she had said she would file (04:03); denial dated 6 April 2026 (05:55), with no notice of intent to deny beforehand (03:25). She says she asked at the time of the approval, "Is this a mistake?", and was told "No, it was the discretion of the officer" (01:11).

  7. ^

    Turfah v. USCIS, 845 F.3d 668 (6th Cir. 2017), slip opinion pp. 4-5: "Every circuit court to consider the lawful-admission requirement has deferred to the BIA's interpretation in Koloamatangi", under which "an alien is not lawfully admitted if he gains LPR status due to a mistake by the government", even without fraud. https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/17a0001p-06.pdf

  8. ^

    The same section lists as an example "USCIS incorrectly approved the applicant's adjustment application" and closes with "The applicant is generally ineligible for naturalization under such circumstances, even if he or she did not commit any fraud". The "generally" is real: section E of the same chapter, "Applicants Considered Lawfully Admitted", lists the errors USCIS does forgive. They are clerical: a visa number not requested or allocated when one was available, a wrong class-of-admission code, and an unpaid INA 245(i) "statutory sum", which may be paid during naturalization if it is the sole problem. Nothing medical. https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-12-part-d-chapter-2

  9. ^

    Turfah, p. 9: "Turfah's circumstances are certainly sympathetic. As Turfah puts it, he is being denied naturalization 'based on a technicality.' This result could be considered unfair, but we are constrained to follow 22 C.F.R. § 40.1(a)(2) and affirm the district court's ruling". The court also defended the rule (p. 8): the accompanying requirement "is not necessarily 'absurd.' One can easily imagine the chaos that would result from allowing a minor child to immigrate months, or even days, before his or her parents", and held that federal courts have no equitable power to confer citizenship (p. 9, citing INS v. Pangilinan).

  10. ^

    The attorney in the video does propose a route (07:16-09:40): request a hearing on the denial (Form N-336) before the 30-day deadline, use it to get in front of a supervisor, and ask USCIS to reopen the original green card case so she can file a new medical. He is explicit about the price: "My punishment is I'm going to get a new green card with a new start date and I'm going to have to wait 3 to 5 years to apply for citizenship again" (07:36), and he rates reopening an approved application without that leverage as "almost impossible" (08:09). Two other lawyers told her to go through removal proceedings and re-apply for a green card in front of the immigration judge, at an estimated $10,000-15,000 (10:53, 13:51). Note also what the denial does not do: it does not cancel her green card. Rescinding permanent residence is a separate proceeding, and 8 U.S.C. 1256(a) allows it only "within five years after the status of a person has been otherwise adjusted" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1256). The Turfah court (pp. 8-9) held that the window closing "simply means that the government cannot institute recission proceedings ... not that Turfah's entry was lawful in the first place". So she is left with a green card that is good enough to live on and not good enough to naturalize from.

  11. ^

    Turfah v. United States Citizenship and Immigration Services, No. 16-1282, 845 F.3d 668 (6th Cir., decided 6 January 2017), opinion by Judge Gilman, concurrence by Judge Boggs, affirming the Eastern District of Michigan (Judge Battani, 2016). Facts from the opinion (p. 2): Turfah, then 19, arrived on 23 September 1995 on a visa for a child "accompanying or following to join" his father; "the immigration authorities mistakenly admitted Turfah"; his father arrived on 17 October 1995 and later became a citizen; Turfah applied for naturalization in November 2012. USCIS originally also denied on a second ground, good moral character over his 2010 taxes, and later dropped it. https://www.opn.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/17a0001p-06.pdf

  12. ^

    Turfah, pp. 9-12. The majority wrote only: "we encourage the government to use any discretion that it might have to overcome the current impasse on Turfah's road to naturalization" (p. 9). The retroactive wording is the district court's, quoted by Judge Boggs (p. 11): the government "may decide whether it is appropriate to issue this status nunc pro tunc, or retroactively." Boggs's own concurrence (pp. 10-12) adds the quotes in the text and ends: "I would therefore encourage USCIS to use any discretion it has in processing a Form I-485, should Turfah choose to file one" (p. 12).

  13. ^

    USCIS, "Number of Service-wide Forms by Quarter, Form Status, and Processing Time", fiscal year 2025 Q4 workbook, sheet FY25Q4_All_Forms, fiscal-year-to-date columns. Fiscal year 2025 runs 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025. All forms: 11,037,994 completions (9,573,826 approved, 1,142,491 denied; receipts 12,981,570). N-400 naturalization applications including the military row: 983,616 completions, 898,050 approved, 85,566 denied, a denial rate of 8.7%. The workbook has no breakdown of denial reasons. https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/data/quarterly_all_forms_fy2025_q4_v1.xlsx . Even USCIS's internal records may not answer the question: a 2022 study of FOIA-obtained N-400 data (2.69 million decisions, October 2014 to March 2018) found that "over 20% of denials in our analytic sample are missing on adjudication reason" and that "denial reasons are not reliably and systematically captured" (Ryo and Humphrey, PNAS 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8892311/).

item.title: AI Marketplaces Can Contribute to, and Profit From, the AI 2040 Plan: Research Directions and Strategy
item.description:
Epistemic status: Draft-Quality. Partially motivated reasoning.

After my “Not Pinning Your OpenRouter Provider Might Invalidate Your Research” post, a representative of an AI marketplace reached out to me about providers and reproducibility. I unofficially chatted with a representative there[1] about this essay, but they do not endorse this document.[2]

This document is entirely human written. Particular research investigations that can be taken by researchers in AI Marketplaces are in bold. I do not currently plan to work more on this project myself, but I wanted to get the idea out so that others might consider it and build on it.

Introduction

AI developers are racing towards recursive self-improvement and artificial superintelligence. If this happens, most likely all of humanity loses control to the AIs or the frontier lab irreversibly concentrates their power.

One faction which currently has not-insignificant power over the AI ecosystem are AI Marketplaces. These are organizations like OpenRouter which do not produce frontier models but generate hundreds of millions in revenue (OpenRouter brings in $140 million in annualized revenue, an estimated $50 million / 5% = $1 billion flows through their marketplace, and they just sold to Stripe for $7 billion) as they connect users to the models and providers best suited to their use cases.

If an AI pause or slowdown were to occur, these AI Marketplaces could continue being profitable and influential for years or decades. If no pause or slowdown occurs, then they will quickly become irrelevant, as superintelligence outcompetes their would-be customers and has no need for AI Marketplaces since it can handle its own compute.[3]

This implies that it is in the personal, commercial, and altruistic interests of AI Marketplaces to facilitate and push for an AI slowdown or pause and to prepare to capitalize on one if one occurs. These are the futures in which most of the value exists for AI Marketplaces.

Certain types of pause would benefit AI Marketplaces more than others. AI Marketplaces benefit from diverse models/providers/usage as that makes routing more useful. If a pause consolidates development in a few existing frontier labs, AI Marketplaces would lose influence and profitability.

A thorough AI pause plan which advocates for a pause at the frontier but encourages the diffusion of AI know-how and the integration of AI into the economy is AI 2040 by the AI Futures Project. This plan has issues which need to be worked out, but it can offer a productive starting point for thinking about how humanity can navigate the future of AI.

This essay analyzes how AI Marketplaces can contribute to and prepare for an AI pause as described in AI 2040. As a brief summary of AI 2040, it describes a recommended “Plan A” in which AI progress is harnessed and provides huge (50% yearly!) GDP growth, but a treaty between the US and China stops AI development from creating out-of-control systems too quickly.

AI 2040 advocates many policy changes, it will take a lot of political will to make them happen, and powerful interests are fighting regulation. AI Marketplaces might be able to help make Plan A happen by doing “Virtuous [Regulatory] Capture”: “When powerful interest groups thwart justified regulation, the optimal strategy for pursuing that regulation may be to indirectly empower interest groups that stand to profit from it in the long-run.”

Some economic advantages an AI Pause would give to AI Marketplaces:

  • Frontier labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI have a lot of bargaining power since they are a duopoly with the best models and users are willing to pay a premium for intelligence. With the frontier paused as in AI 2040, there will be a larger number of frontier providers and AI Marketplaces will have more bargaining power.
  • AI Marketplaces can become the intermediaries between customers and the cheap, personalized intelligence driving all economic development. This could grant them the role as the “Amazon” of the 2030s.

Some political advantages that virtuous regulatory capture would give marketplaces:

  • If the government mandates AI Marketplaces implement changes, then the marketplace with foresight will be prepared and competitors will have to scramble. Exemplary AI Marketplaces can push the government to mandate good behavior, making things harder for less scrupulous competition.
  • The government would be more likely to partner with an AI Marketplace that has implemented the features they want. This can mean billion-dollar government contracts.

Actions AI Marketplaces Could Take Now

Provider Implementation Transparency

AI2040 advocates Full Research Transparency where all research becomes open-source.[4] AI Marketplaces can incentivize model providers to open-source their inference setups, setting up “Prize Systems” which incentivize innovation as an alternative to trade secrets. Already, there is demand for providers to be more transparent about how they are running their models because the lack of openness interferes with scientific reproducibility and makes it difficult to know what object is being studied. Additionally, if implementations were open, costs would go down for consumers, and there would be less risk of switching from one provider to another with the same implementation. AI Marketplaces should gauge interest from customers for how valuable customers would find open implementations and calculate how much value the second order effects would provide to the marketplace. The AI Marketplace can run a test, offering to pay providers to share their implementation with the Marketplace and with other providers who agree not to share the implementation externally. The marketplace representative told me that  “providers see their implementation as their alpha” but I still argue that there is some price at which they would be willing to sell it, and AI Marketplaces should find that price. Additionally, since there are many model providers for some models (almost 20 for GPT-OSS-120B) I would expect AI Marketplaces to be able to find a seller among them. The marketplace representative thinks that this requires too much buy-in, overhead, and trust towards untrusted providers. He prefers weights/quantization, versioning, parameter conformance, change notices, and verification as better targets. I consider this insufficient for scientific reproducibility, and under the AI 2040 Plan A, this would be insufficiently open.

Compute Tracking

An important step for an AI pause is for the parties of the treaties to know the location of all (or the significant majority) of the world’s compute. AI Marketplaces can and should use their data to infer lower bounds for how much compute each of their providers controls. An AI Marketplace could also incentivise providers to disclose their amount of compute and to install verification devices to prove that the chips are only used for inference rather than training. This information would be invaluable for a possible treaty, and if an AI Marketplace implemented these changes, they would be politically well-positioned.

Preventing Misuse

This idea may be controversial among those who work at AI Marketplaces, but it is worth considering: Bad actors and rogue AIs will demand vast quantities of inference. Governments are likely to want to be able to keep track of AI usage, mandating know-your-customer and risk-tiered access. I don’t see anything in the OpenRouter terms of service involving know-your-customer, and OpenRouter does not seem to operate a Customer Identification Program. AI Marketplaces can get a better idea of who is using their AI while maintaining the privacy in what they are using AI to do. As a concrete example, AI Marketplaces should review their data to see if there is a concerning amount of frontier bio-capable model usage in unstable regions of the world, potentially indicating bioweapons projects[5]. If AI Marketplace data has the potential to identify and predict the next COVID-scale pandemic, someone should certainly look into it.

The marketplace representative says that this part is directionally interesting and that as models get more powerful, marketplaces will likely need stronger identity requirements and high-risk usage classifiers. He says that each of the following needs to be elaboration to be actionable for them: KYC, classifier-based enforcement, aggregate regional analysis, actual threat detection, what signals are collected, what gets retained, how false positives are handled, and what actions to take when something gets flagged.

Chain-of-Thought Monitorability

Chain-of-thought monitorability is an important component of oversight, and it varies by model and by provider. AI Marketplaces should analyze their data to figure out how important chain-of-thought monitorability is to their customers. This can be done by surveying customers and analyzing consumer preferences when controlling for other aspects of model desiderata. They can then test the chain of thought monitorability of models and providers and see how user behavior changes when given this information in an A/B test. By giving customers the option to choose greater chain-of-thought monitorability, they create incentives for model providers and developers to keep chain-of-thought monitorable.

Model Specs

Transparency is core to the AI 2040 Plan A. Researchers and governments need to be able to have observability into what is going on in order to study the safety of near-superhuman AI and ensure that all parties are holding to the terms of the treaties. AI Marketplaces can contribute to this by incentivizing companies to “publicly report their model specifications (detailed documentation about what goals/values they are attempting to train their AIs to follow).” I imagine that model users already want this information to be available. AI Marketplaces can link to model specifications on their model pages, and if no such spec exists, they can clearly flag that absence in a way which discourages use. It would be interesting to A/B test this visibility feature to see how much users value visible, thorough model specifications.

Conclusion

AI Marketplaces are big believers in the power of intelligence, and their companies are built around that value. At the same time, they need to think hard about what the future will look like and which of those futures they prefer, both from a business perspective and from the perspective of members of humanity. Good futures involve humanity achieving geopolitical cooperation, good incentives, and a better understanding of AI. AI Marketplaces are both well-positioned and well-incentivized to contribute to humanity’s path toward a good outcome.

item.title: Rogue AI developers as hostis humani generis: under an international AI treaty, should they be subject to international concurrent jurisdiction?
item.description:
An international treaty banning superhuman AI will, necessarily, require the arrest of rogue AI developers who violate the treaty. But who should be authorized to conduct these arrests? Should there be some sort of international concurrent jurisdiction, allowing at least some countries to conduct arrests of defectors within other countries’ territory?

The default approach - allowing countries to make such arrests only within their own borders - may quickly cause the treaty to fall apart. If national governments operate under the thesis that anyone who achieves superhuman AI (artificial superintelligence, or ASI) will immediately have dominion over the rest of the world, any government has reason to defect and begin racing to build ASI if they even suspect any other country is also defecting (for instance, by choosing not to arrest their own citizens who are defecting and racing to ASI). As a result, bad intelligence collection by a single country could lead to the collapse of the treaty, even with nobody actually defecting beforehand.

Another approach is inspired by the hostis humani generis doctrine applied to pirates during the Age of Sail, in which any seagoing country had the right to interdict pirates and try the pirates in their own admiralty courts, regardless of the pirates’ nationality. Under this system, any country would be permitted to conduct arrests of rogue AI developers within any other such country, even though this would mean operating unilaterally within another country’s territory. This solves the previous approach’s core problem, but introduces many new problems of its own. One country might decide to fabricate evidence, or use spurious evidence, as justification to arrest all of another leading country’s known AI researchers. Forces of one country operating on another country’s territory unannounced, or with short notice, could easily lead to a completely unnecessary shooting war that a better-structured treaty would avoid entirely. The original hostis humani generis doctrine applied to pirates at sea; arresting another country’s pirates in international waters is a much less fraught matter than arresting another country’s AI researchers within that country itself.

As both of those approaches fail, an alternative is needed. I propose that a broad coalition of middle powers, independent of the US and China, stand up and maintain a well-trained, well-resourced force capable of making such arrests across borders. All countries would be bound by treaty to tolerate this force’s operations within their own borders, under certain criteria. This coalition itself would appoint a smaller set of mediator countries, with long and trusted records of fair dealing in fraught geopolitical circumstances, to adjudicate evidence and determine whether the middle powers’ force may proceed with any particular action.

Full analysis here: https://connorsscratchpad.substack.com/p/rogue-ai-developers-hostis-humani

item.title: Why are some explanations bad?
item.description:
I like understanding things. Many explanations strike me as insufficient, and I wanted to know what features characterize the explanations that frustrate me. I looked through answers to why questions on Quora, found ones I didn’t like, and tried to find patterns in them. So far, I've come up with the following ways that explanations can go wrong:


Insufficient specificity

Often, when I'm asking a why question, a general answer will not satisfy my confusion or curiosity. It’s common, though, to not answer specifically enough, ranking as my top complaint with explanations I looked at on Quora.

Here are some examples of cases where an explanation lacks contrast:

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why do people believe in the supernatural?

Because they have confirmation bias

Any belief can be related to confirmation bias. What about supernatural beliefs make it more related to confirmation bias than others?

Why do people scroll social media?

Because they get dopamine from doing that

Any behavior could be explained in these terms. What is special about social media?

Why are plants green?

Because they emit wavelengths in the range of 495–570 nm

All green things emit those wavelengths!

Why do shot-for-shot remakes exist?

Profit (based on this)

Any movie could be made with profit in mind. A more complete answer could be:

Shot-for-shot remakes are especially profitable because they walk the line of peoples’ preferences for familiarity and nostalgia with novelty. Most people wouldn’t watch the exact same movie twice in theaters, but they are more interested in a new movie if it’s something they’re already familiar with. 


Interestingly, not all questions should be answered with the specificity that the question asker is looking for. Here are some examples:

Question

Explanation

Why does Bill have four legs?

Because he’s a cat and cats have four legs.

Why do men commit more murders than women?

Because men commit more violence in general. 

Why does [plant species] have chlorophyll?

Because nearly every plant species has chlorophyll. 

At first, I didn't think these were good explanations because patterns are not causal. Being a cat doesn't cause an animal to have four legs. Still, these explanations add relevant information that can clear things up for the question-asker.

Insufficient acknowledgement of counterexamples

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why do animals like polar bears have thick fur?

Because they need to keep warm (based on this)

This is an okay answer, but not all arctic animals have thick fur. A better answer could be:

Many arctic animals have layers of thick fur, but others have blubber. While blubber is more energetically expensive, hair can become compressed in water, making it ineffective as insulation.

Why don’t sharks have bones?

“Bones are rigid and fixed in length after a species specific period. Cartilage is flexible and can increase in size as critters like sharks continue to grow throughout their lives.” (from this)

Large bony fish exist, too.

To get more specifity, you can try asking questions like:

  • Why do ___ have ___ rather than some other trait?
  • Why do ___ have ___, but others in the same category don’t have this trait?
  • Why __________? Is there a different mechanism behind this than others in the same category?


Insufficient mechanistic detail

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why is the flame from a gas stove blue?

Blue flames are produced by excited radicals.

I don’t know anything about how radicals would emit light, so I would still be pretty confused.

Interestingly, the following is sufficient for me when it comes to why some flames are orange, suggesting that analogous situations are important:

Soot particles at really high temperatures, similarly to a hot metal, glow orange.

Why does rain fall as small drops?

Because of air resistance (based on this) 

To me, it’s not intuitive how air resistance would make raindrops smaller. I think this could be solved with a good analogy.

Asking for intuitive examples or analogies may help with this problem.

Not the kind of explanation I wanted

There may be a variety of true answers to a “why” question, but they may not all be what you’re looking for. The question "Why are plants green?" can be answered from a variety of perspectives:

Category

Explanation?

Cause?

Before effect?

Example

Historical

Yes

Yes

Yes

Plants are green because an ancestral cell engulfed a photosynthetic cell, which eventually became the chloroplast.

Evolutionary

Yes

Yes

Yes

Plants are green because chlorophyll-based organisms may have outcompeted retinal-based ones, making a chlorophyll-using organism more likely to become the endosymbiotic ancestor of chloroplasts.

Mechanism

Yes

Maybe

No

Plants are green because they contain chlorophyll, which reflects green wavelengths and absorbs others.

Definition

No

No

-

Plants are green because they are perceived as the color we call green.  

Pattern

No

No

Most plants have some green parts.

Interestingly, while the mechanistic answer is most common for the above question, it's often not mechanisms that we're looking for with why questions (usually, that's "how"). 


Here’s an example of an answer that doesn’t address the kind of answer I’m looking for:

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why don’t more animals eat wood?

Wood contains lignin, which is difficult to break down.

I want it to address something about an evolutionary tradeoff, like:

Wood contains lignin, which is difficult to break down. There are tradeoffs when it comes to processing lignin: it’s abundant, but it’s physically hard, requires a lot of specialized chemical machinery to break down and use as energy, and the chemical machinery involves highly reactive molecules.


It can help when asking a question to think about what kind of explanation you’re looking for. Here’s some ideas:

Category

Subcategory

Example questions

Historical

Historical origin

What is the historical origin of _____?

Evolutionary

Arbitrary/ random

Why is _____ so common? Was it beneficial or selected for, due to random chance, linked to something that was adaptive, or a spandrel?

What is the evolutionary tradeoff related to ___?

Adaptive/ beneficial

Genetic hitchhiking

Spandrel

Mechanism

Mechanism

What is the mechanism underlying _____  at the [cellular/ atomic/ etc.] level?


Circular or semantic

Next, there are circular and semantic explanations. For "why are plants green?" you could answer "they are the color we call green." I don't think these are super common, and I didn’t find examples of this on Quora.

Question

Insufficient explanation

Why do people look for evidence that confirms their beliefs?

Because they have confirmation bias.


Miscellaneous problems

Question

Insufficient explanation

Problem

Why is Pluto no longer considered a planet?

Because Pluto shares its orbital area with many other objects.

Did the definition change, or did we learn something new about Pluto? If the definition changed, was it for a particular reason? Does the new definition draw a line that reflects reality?

Why are wolves considered evil?

Because we learn to think of them as evil as children through fairytales.

Confuses correlation with causation; why did people make them evil in fairytales?

Why don’t other sharks normally grow as large as great white sharks?

“Short answer is that they are different species.” (from this)

I would want something related to ecological tradeoffs… This doesn’t even provide new information.


Explanations are overrated

While I've focused here on explanations, which are often causal, I think we might spend too much of our limited attention focused on causality. Patterns and descriptions can, and do, help us make decisions.

For instance, imagine you have a symptom that is highly correlated with having a particular disease. If we have a treatment for that disease, it makes sense to test for that disease based on this correlation. Another example: I’ve performed a couple weeks of extensive mood tracking, finding that most evenings and weekends I have pretty high moods, while I have lower moods at work. It made me think that, if I could find things to improve my mood at work, that would have a much larger impact on my overall happiness than trying hobbies I might enjoy more.

Modern science produces lots of experiments and other non-experiments trying to make causal claims. Some have critiqued this movement away from descriptive research (i.e. Grimaldi & Engel 2007). As an example of fascinating and modern descriptive work, Patty Brennan’s career has been centered on animal genitalia, and I would highly recommend this video or this article. 


Understanding things requires a mix of descriptive and causal information. Perhaps my desire to understand focuses too much on the latter, as even this essay is an attempt to see what causes me to not like certain explanations.


Thank you to my friends for providing me with feedback! :)

item.title: Hindsight: a trivia + calibration game
item.description:
I made a betting game called Hindsight (AI slop rulebook at https://hindsight.markets/rules). At last year’s Metagame conference I playtested a face-to-face version but ultimately we gave up trying to come up with methods to trade the chips around conveniently.

The online version is a “TV party game” like JackBox where players view public info on a common screen and private info and decisions on their phones.

Each player starts with 100 chips. The game progresses in a series of rounds until all players but one are bankrupted. In each round there’s a hidden target year between 1900 and 1999. The round has three stages and during each stage:

  1. A clue is revealed about the year—a birth, death, or event (“Grand Rapids, Michigan becomes the first city in the world to add fluoride to its public drinking water”).
  2. There’s an auction in which the players bid down how wide a market they’re willing to make (“I’ll quote a market six years wide”… “I’ll do four”…).
  3. Then the market maker presents a bid and ask price and everyone else must buy or sell N contracts with the market maker where N is the round number. (The escalating stakes prevent the game from going on forever.)

After all three stages, the year is revealed and the contracts settle at one chip per year of distance. The slop rulebook includes other details like who eats the losses when someone goes bankrupt.

item.title: Some interesting internal documents from Anthropic litigation
item.description:
Anthropic released some documents earlier this year due to the book copyright litigation. I think a few of those documents might be of interest to some people here and haven't gotten much attention. In this post I link to some of those documents, and quote the bits I find interesting.[1] (This expands on my quick take from yesterday.)

These aren't Anthropic's official opinions about anything, and you should probably treat opinions in these documents as "what the author thought at the time", not as a corporate stance.

Concise Research Roadmap

It describes Anthropic's research plans in July 2021:[2]

Long Term Goal 

Our top level goal is to work towards the creation of safe, beneficial AGI.

As a proof of concept, we are working to develop a general AI assistant that can interact conversationally with a user to create, edit, and explain software. The most ambitious and successful version of this agent could answer general questions, write functions, identify bugs, design an API, discuss style and best practices, etc -- it would display all the capabilities of a software engineer colleague. We don't expect to reach this goal right away, but it's the direction in which we're striving. 

Our research projects can all be viewed as attempts to understand and construct aspects of this proto-AGI. We currently think this will require large generative models with long memories, fine tuned via RL using both automated rewards and human feedback.

In the pretraining section:

Study the science of:

  • ML advances needed to train arbitrarily large models (1T and larger) while well-optimizing their capabilities for future use and further finetuning
  • Very large contexts (or some equivalent to pack in a great deal of memory/experience)
  • Data quality, including filtering, transfer, finetuning, and diversity, setting the stage for comparisons with RL environments relevant for more advanced models

It predicted the usefulness of RL for tool use pretty early:

RL for Tool Use

Primary goals:

  • Advance our understanding of the path to AGI by exploring the ability of large LMs to use tools and learn about / generate data about their environments and goals
  • See clear signs of life on search, printf debugging, and other valuable tasks, evaluate whether tool use and RL are dissolving the limitations of current large LMs
  • Identify training techniques that produce a more favorable scaling with training compute as compared to supervised learning

Another employee's comments on that document:

I'm a bit nervous if we end up doing alignment research on natural language and capabilities research on code. It feels like there should be a pretty tight connection between the two at all times. If we're not improving capabilities in the domains we're doing alignment research on, it puts limits on how much we can test alignment and how useful the alignment work can be. That could have knock-on effects like alignment becoming an island because we don't integrate it early on.

A possible principle: "by default, capabilities and alignment research should be in proportion across domains unless we can give a good argument for why they should come apart". Is this a good/bad principle?

Data Hypotheses

It describes hypotheses (the author doesn't "believe any of them with very high probability") about what training data is useful. Among other things, it suggests training on Chinese text to slow down Chinese AI labs:

The China Competition Hypothesis – China seems like it might be the least ethical / safe AI actor. To the extent we can slow them down by absorbing market share they could grab (and thereby use to accelerate production of large models), we can tip the geopolitical balance. As a result, we should prioritize having good linguistic performance on languages for markets Chinese companies might be inclined to go after – Mandarin (although Chinese government intervention will likely push us out here), but perhaps also neighbors or countries deeply involved in the Belt and Road strategy.

A comment on the doc:

Some related comments from @ben@anthropic.com --

  • Chinese may still be valuable for all the Chinese diaspora/expats
  • +1 transfer knowledge from Chinese to English
  • Unlikely China will enforce copyright on US?
  • US gov’t may be interested in Chinese language ability for national security reasons, if we end up engaging there

All Company meeting!

This is a June 2021 slideshow[3] that discusses hiring, office space, the efficiency of training trillion parameter models, RL, sources of training data, and interpretability. It discusses Anthropic's first alignment failure in the "RL Update" section:

  • Now running simplest-possible tool-use env
  • Codewhack:
    • Agent gets some words from a Github repo
    • Agent needs to pick a search query that gets exactly one hit.
  • Seemed to work! But,

[next slide]

  • Actually our first alignment failure.
  • Examples:
    • " script that looks at instargram" => "^"
    • " = img.shape[:2]\n\n " => "^"
    • "docker.utils.mkbuildcontext(" => "^"
  • What’s happening?
    • “^” is the regex start of sequence token.
    • There’s only one start of sequence!
    • I didn’t escape the query.
    • I did not end the universe. This time.

Product visions for early 2025 (written in June 2023)

It discusses potential use-cases for Claude 18 months in the future, as of June 2023. At the bottom (in the blue text[4]), various Anthropic employees provide their own takes.

It suggests setting an ambitious goal (transformative AI) and breaking it down into stepping stones that show progress and profit along the way, like SpaceX:

We'll want to find clear stepping stones between where we are now and the long term vision, where we get technological proof points and market feedback along the way. Companies like Magic Leap that aim straight for their super-ambitious final destination end up disconnected from reality and burn an obscene amount of money, ultimately falling behind competitors who were able to absorb market feedback and build organizational muscle. SpaceX is probably a great example of doing this right. The founders (yes, there's more than one!) had the borderline ridiculous goal of achieving human settlement on Mars, but they broke it down into a series of steps that achieved proof points and profit along the way. First they got good at building small, profitable, low cost rockets, then they got good at building medium sized, profitable, low cost rockets, then they figured out how to make rockets reusable to further lower the cost, then they became the world's largest provider of orbital launch capability with their superior product, then they built the world's largest rocket and almost got it into space on the first try… and if they can generate enough demand for heavy lift launch capability, then they can mass produce these giant rockets and start sending them to Mars. The long term goal kept the team inspired and focused, and the steps along the way gave the team the skills and the revenue to succeed.

It discusses "three major visions for TAI": "Claude the Virtual Employee" (also called "Claude the Robot"), "Claude the personal assistant" (also "Claude the Cyborg"), and "Claude as intelligent org infrastructure". It says working on Claude the Virtual Employee and Claude as org infrastructure are useful to "reduce TAI risk", and Claude the personal assistant is "Sort of" useful for reducing TAI risk.

Responsible Scaling as a Framework for Anthropic

It is a slideshow that discusses the RSP and why Anthropic scales capabilities.

Interpretability & Alignment, or Bankruptcy

  • Sometimes folks ask if product is just here to "fund alignment & interpretability research"...
  • But you can also argue for the opposite:
    • In worlds where alignment is extremely difficult or impossible, these teams need to save the world by demonstrating this fact persuasively
    • In worlds where alignment is easy/manageable, these teams need to save the company by making responsible scaling well-defined and achievable

This is a bit of an exaggeration, but not too much. We're all working together to accomplish a common mission.

It has a diagram of Anthropic's business model:


Slack messages

I had Claude make a thingie to read Slack messages from the filings.

  • These are mostly uninteresting.
  • Teal = Claude 3 Opus, Dove/Firefly/Wombat = Claude 3.5/3.6/3.7 Sonnet according to Anthropic's table.[5]

Conclusion

Keep in mind that these documents weren't intended to be public, they aren't Anthropic's official position on anything, and were written in the past. I don't want anyone to get the impression that any of these documents represent commitments from Anthropic to do anything; instead you should think of these as information about what some people at Anthropic were thinking about in the past.

Also keep in mind that this isn't a random sample of documents. The documents Anthropic releases due to litigation are strongly tilted towards being about training data because Anthropic gets sued over their training data a lot, and doesn't get a lot of lawsuits related to things like alignment science. You should also consider that Anthropic might try harder to redact information that makes them look bad. Most of the documents I looked at are things like Data Partnerships <> Finance; Monthly Syncs which is heavily redacted and much less interesting.[6]

Thanks to Anthropic and the authors of these documents for creating them; I enjoyed reading them! Also thanks to the Free Law Project for running RECAP/CourtListener, which is where I got these documents from. (Perhaps I should get a PACER account so I can access documents that aren't already in RECAP.)

I'll probably get back to focusing on technical alignment research now, but reading obscure documents about Anthropic has been a fun hobby!
